about.title: Newport Beach Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Not every disappointing result in a hospital or clinic is malpractice, and Newport Beach residents deserve a straight answer about the difference. Under California's MICRA rules, a claim requires showing that a provider fell below the accepted standard of care and that the lapse caused harm, which is why a qualified medical expert is almost always required. The timeline is unforgiving: generally one year from the date you discovered the injury, and never more than three years from when it happened, with a 90-day notice sent to the provider before any lawsuit is filed. Orange County patients also run into MICRA's cap on non-economic damages, a figure that rises each year rather than staying fixed. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects people in Newport Beach with an independent attorney who handles medical negligence cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery. Whether your case began with a routine visit or with emergency care after a crash on Jamboree Road, an early review costs you nothing.

whyChoose.title: Why Newport Beach Patients Start With LawProactive

items.title: The MICRA clock is short
items.desc: You generally have one year from discovering the injury, and never more than three years from the injury itself, plus a 90-day pre-suit notice must go out first. An early connection keeps those dates from slipping.

items.title: An expert opinion is nearly always required
items.desc: A bad outcome alone is not malpractice under California law. The independent attorneys in our network know how to line up a qualified medical expert who can evaluate whether the standard of care was actually breached.

items.title: The damages cap changes every year
items.desc: MICRA limits non-economic damages, but that limit rises annually. An attorney who tracks the current figure can explain honestly what your claim may and may not include, without promising a result.

items.question: I was treated at a hospital near Newport Beach after a car crash on Coast Highway. Can I pursue a malpractice claim on top of the crash claim?
items.answer: Sometimes, yes. A collision claim against the other driver and a malpractice claim against a provider are separate matters with different deadlines and different proof requirements. Because MICRA imposes its own one-year discovery rule and a 90-day notice step, it helps to have an attorney look at both timelines together rather than assuming one covers the other.

items.question: My surgery did not fix the problem. Does that mean I have a case?
items.answer: Not by itself. California law asks whether the provider fell below the accepted standard of care and whether that failure caused your harm, and a qualified medical expert is almost always needed to answer that. A poor result with proper care is not malpractice; a poor result caused by a preventable error may be.
